issues: Re-fetched arXiv 2507.12844. --check FOUND. The abstract page's submission history shows v1 on Thu 17 Jul 2025 and v2 on 12 Nov 2025. The unversioned /pdf URL serves v2, and the same sentence is also in v1, so the 2025-07-17 date holds. Section 4.2.1 tested three models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Gemini 2.0 Flash, 10 trials each per banner) on a clone of one news site (Tiroler Tageszeitung). 'LLM web agents' with no qualifier generalizes a single-site, three-model test, so the explanation now names the setting.

The ChatGPT agent page's context reads 'With a single click in ChatGPT's settings, you can delete all browsing data and immediately log out of all active website sessions. Otherwise, cookies persist based on each visited website's cookie policies'. 'Keeps cookies' is right, but only unless the user clears them. That qualifier is added.

Operator: the page says Operator 'asks the user to take over' as a safety design, and calls it 'one of our first agents'. 'Had to hand the keyboard back' reads as a forced limitation. It is reworded to what the page says.

'Consent ... has no defined meaning when software performs it' is overstated. The GDPR already contemplates consent through technical settings (Recital 32) and objection 'by automated means' (Art. 21(5)). What has no settled meaning is an AI agent clicking 'accept' on a person's behalf. The explanation is softened to say that.
The Wayback sources (index 1 and 2) could not be re-fetched live (see the notes). Their quotes and context were confirmed today from the cached copy of the same capture URLs.

fieldFixes.explanation: In a controlled test on a cloned news site, three LLM web agents (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Gemini 2.0 Flash) facing cookie banners never opened the granular settings - they accepted everything or nothing. OpenAI's ChatGPT agent keeps cookies 'based on each visited website's cookie policies' unless the user clears its browsing data, and its earlier browsing agent, Operator, asks the human to take over when login credentials or payment details are needed. Consent designed as a human ceremony has no settled meaning when an AI agent performs it on a person's behalf.

issues: All three quotes --check FOUND 2026-09-23. The IEEE SA page gives 'Board Approval 2025-11-04', 'Published: 2026-01-20' and 'PAR Approval 2017-12-06', with Doc Searls as Working Group Chair. The myterms.info agreements page was modified 2026-01-22 (JSON-LD dateModified).

'IEEE 7012 is written for exactly this' overstates. The PAR dates from 2017, and in the scope sentence 'AI agents' are listed among the service providers individuals engage (second parties), not as the person's own agent. The abstract separately provides that 'Computing devices and software performing as agents for both first and second parties shall engage using any protocol', and that the first party points to terms chosen from 'a roster kept by an independent and neutral non-business entity'. The explanation is reworded to keep these roles straight.

'Without it, the only terms an agent can carry are each site's own' overstates. Agents can already carry one-bit signals such as GPC, which are legally binding in California and Colorado. It is narrowed to contractual terms.

fieldFixes.explanation: IEEE 7012 provides for this. It covers agreements between individuals and the service providers they engage, 'including websites, applications and AI agents'. The individual, acting as first party, points to standard-form terms chosen from a roster kept by an independent, neutral non-business entity, and software agents may act for either side. MyTerms describes SD-BASE as the default agreement for 'any individual using an agent'. Without such a standard, the only contractual terms an agent meets are each site's own.

'Colorado has enforced a universal opt-out since July 2024' is imprecise. The Colorado AG says controllers 'will be required to accept opt-out requests through universal opt-out mechanisms starting on July 1, 2024'. That is an obligation, and no enforcement action was verified. It is reworded.

'Dropped from the Council's June 2026 text' had no source in this record, and the Council text itself was not read. noyb (FOUND: 'In the proposal for a final vote in the Council, Article 88b was removed entirely from the Digital Omnibus') and the 10 Sep 2026 coalition letter (FOUND: it asks the Irish presidency 'to re-insert Article 88b into their next compromise text') are added. fieldFixes.explanation: The GDPR already lets people object 'by automated means using technical specifications'. California's regulations make businesses that sell or share personal information treat opt-out preference signals as valid requests. AB 566 obliges browser makers to offer such a signal from 1 January 2027, and Colorado has required businesses to accept universal opt-out signals since 1 July 2024. The EU's proposed Article 88b would require controllers to accept automated, machine-readable consent choices. The EDPB and EDPS strongly welcomed it, but according to noyb it was removed from the Council's 18 June 2026 text.

fieldFixes.explanation: In an urgent March 2023 order, Italy's regulator noted the absence of an adequate legal basis for training ChatGPT on personal data. The EUR 15 million fine that followed in 2024 was overturned when the Court of Rome upheld OpenAI's appeal in March 2026. The EU's pending Digital Omnibus proposal would let AI development rest on 'legitimate interests' plus an unconditional right to object. Machine-readable AI signals so far serve content owners (robots.txt, AIPREF, RSL, Cloudflare). MyTerms' PDC-AI agreement lets an individual affirmatively offer specific data 'for the purposes of Training and Operating AI technologies' on their own terms. Meanwhile 30% of GenAI users in Cisco's 2024 12-country survey say they already enter personal or confidential information into these tools.

fieldFixes.response: The MyTerms project concedes that its agreements 'will take time to propagate and not all organisations will adopt them', and says its first targets are sites 'that don't participate in the surveillance economy'. Adoption therefore likely depends on regulatory pressure or on accepting sites gaining trust. The nearest EU lever, the proposed Article 88b on machine-readable privacy choices, covers consent signals rather than full terms, and according to noyb it was removed from the Council's June 2026 text. We found no public adoption data as of September 2026.
